summary_out.changed: Cold-start G1L1 from the `simple` template: added a two-signal microstructure SKIP gate combining Lipton's static top-of-book imbalance I=(q_b-q_a)/(q_b+q_a) with Kolm's rolling per-quote-tick Order Flow Imbalance (OFI, level 1) — skip an opening BUY only when both I>0.33 AND OFI summed over the last 2.0s is >+5 contracts (mirror for SELL). Closing orders always submit; standard anti-cascade flag.
summary_out.outcome: pnl -452.88% vs simple base (-$550.50 vs +$156.00 over 12 train dates), sharpe -1.97 vs +0.60, is_weighted_bps -16.18% (genuinely lower arrival-mid IS cost on the entries that DID fire), trade_count -7.17% (126931 vs 136734) — gate fired on ~7% of opens. mean_slippage 0.0 on both sides (artifact: pure marketable arrival-mid). FAIL — far below the +5.0% pass gate.
summary_out.hypothesis: Passive-posting literature's notion of 'adverse selection at high imbalance' (Lipton's calibrated curves showing ~90% unfavorable-tick probability at |I|≈0.8) should transfer to marketable execution: skipping the moments when both static imbalance and recent OFI agree against the trade direction should improve net PnL by avoiding the worst arrival prices.
summary_out.next: The hypothesis was sign-inverted for marketable orders against a 30s-horizon oracle: strong same-direction I+OFI is *favorable* over 30s (the oracle's actual horizon), not adverse — Lipton's adverse-selection framing is about *passive posting at the near side*, where queue depletion hurts you while you wait. Two strictly better G1L2 candidates: (1) flip the sign — treat strong same-direction I+OFI as a 'must-fire' signal and only skip when the local tape opposes the trade direction; (2) move from binary skip to passive child placement (post LIMIT at near side when |I| moderate, cross spread when |I| extreme in trade direction). Cross-island corollary: 'microstructure signal → SKIP' rules from the passive-posting literature do not transfer to marketable execution against multi-second alphas — other islands should be wary of importing them naively.
